# The Build Order for Professional Services Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-professional-services-firms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Professional services firms run The Build Order almost unchanged, with one addition: confidentiality and conflict walls arrive with the context layer, not after it. The commercial line is the pitch, the fee quote and the go or no-go decision. Utilisation pressure makes Gateway 0 the hardest gate, and fee realisation gives Gateway 2 its dollar figure.

Law, accounting and consulting firms can run The Build Order almost as written. The commercial line is real and well defined: which work to pitch for, what fee to quote, and which write-offs to accept. What changes is the wiring. The same partners who win the work also deliver it, so their inboxes hold both pitch context and client confidences, and the conflict walls a regulator already expects must be built into the context layer on day one. The evidence says firms are using AI faster than they can measure it. Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey of more than 1,500 professionals found 40% say their organisation uses generative AI, while only 18% say it tracks return on investment. Billable utilisation fell to 66.4% in 2025 in SPI Research's benchmark, which makes the protected time Gateway 0 requires unusually expensive to give.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This is the first of four industry editions of The Build Order. Each runs the full sequence (Gateway 0, tooling, context, record, reasoning and Gateways 1 to 3) for one sector, using that sector's regulators, surveys and failure modes. In *The RFP nobody can answer yet* we said the order holds in professional services, with one qualification: confidentiality and conflict walls arrive with the context layer. This piece explains what that means in practice.

Professional services is the sector the series was first drawn from, so it is a useful baseline. Pitches are discrete, the CRM maps reasonably well to how the business runs, and the decisions worth recording are easy to name. The difficulty is not finding the commercial line. It is keeping the commercial line from absorbing everything else a partner knows.

## Where the commercial line sits

In a law firm, an accounting practice or a consultancy, revenue arrives through a small number of repeated decisions. A partner decides whether to pursue a tender or a referral. Someone sets a fee estimate, fixed or hourly, and decides how far to discount it. After the work, someone decides how much of the recorded time to write off. Around those sit panel reviews, cross-selling choices and the conflict check that decides whether the firm can act at all.

| Lens | What it looks like in professional services |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Pursue-or-pass on pitches, fee estimates, discounts and write-offs |
| Store | Practice management system, CRM (often thin), proposal library, partner inboxes |
| Outcome lag | Weeks for a pitch result; one billing cycle for realisation |
| Who defends the decision | Practice heads, the managing partner, finance |
| Main regulator or code | Bar and law society rules, the SRA in England and Wales, accounting ethics codes |
| The wall | Client confidences and conflicts: one client's matter must never inform another's pitch |
| Gateway that bites | Gateway 0: protected time and a CRM partners will keep current |

Those decisions pass the test we set out in *Where judgment arrives first*. They are frequent (a mid-size firm makes several pursue-or-pass calls a week), similar to past cases, graded quickly and defended by someone who owns a budget or a practice. They also produce a clean outcome field. A pitch is won or lost. A fee is realised or written down.

The weak spot is the store. Many firms keep their most valuable relationship data in partner inboxes and the practice management system rather than in a CRM. The CRM, where it exists, records contacts and marketing lists but not the reasoning behind a pitch decision. That is the first thing the build has to fix.

## What the evidence says

The sector's own survey data describes firms that have adopted AI faster than they have learned to govern or measure it.

Thomson Reuters' 2026 AI in Professional Services Report surveyed more than 1,500 professionals across legal, tax, accounting, risk, fraud and government. Forty per cent said their organisation uses generative AI, up from 22% a year earlier. Only 18% said their organisation tracks return on investment, and 40% did not know whether it was measured at all. Fifteen per cent reported agentic AI in use, with another 53% planning or considering it. Two-thirds of corporate respondents want their outside firms to use AI, but fewer than 20% require it. Clients are signalling interest, not setting terms, which leaves firms to decide what to build first.

The economics add pressure. SPI Research's Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, published with Deltek, put billable utilisation at 66.4% in 2025, which it describes as a near two-decade low, down from 73.2% in 2021. EBITDA averaged 9.9% against a benchmark expectation of 15%. Firms are under pressure to find hours, and the temptation is to buy assistant seats for everyone and hope the hours appear. Part 6, *Which AI assistant, which seats*, makes the case for buying seats only for the people in the first workflow.

The regulators have been specific about responsibility. The American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512, issued in July 2024, applies the duties of competence, communication, fees, confidentiality and supervision to generative AI. It says informed client consent may be required before client information goes into a self-learning tool, and that fees must reflect time actually worked. In England and Wales, the Divisional Court's June 2025 judgment in *Ayinde* and *Al-Haroun* found that 18 of 45 authorities cited in one case did not exist. The court said managing partners and heads of chambers must take practical and effective measures to make sure everyone providing legal services understands their duties when using AI.

Taken together: clients want AI used, regulators hold leadership accountable for how it is used, and most firms cannot yet say what it returns. A build that starts with recorded commercial decisions answers all three.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in professional services | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | A named owner with protected hours, the suite of record, a CRM partners will update, and a data-access approver (usually the general counsel or risk partner) | The owner is a fee earner whose protected hours are the first to go |
| Tooling | Assistant seats for business development staff and the partners who pitch most, plus capture of email and meetings into the CRM | Firm-wide seats with no first job |
| Context | Proposals, credentials, CRM and pitch email connected, with information barriers mirrored from the conflicts system | Partner inboxes connect pitch context and client confidences in one place |
| Record | Pursue-or-pass decisions and fee estimates, each with reason, owner, expected fee and check date | Recording only the wins |
| Reasoning | A first agent that assembles pitch preparation packs from approved credentials and the record | The agent quotes a confidential matter as a credential |
| Gateway 1 | Nothing reaches a client or prospect without a named partner's approval, logged | Approval becomes a signature on a draft nobody checked |
| Gateway 2 | Expected fee recorded at pitch; realised fee written back at final bill | Realisation is held in finance and never joined to the pitch |
| Gateway 3 | The record extends to staffing, delivery and finance, with walls intact | Delivery files flood the commercial context |

**Gateway 0.** The three standing decisions apply: an owner, the suite (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) and the CRM. Professional services firms should add the fourth decision that regulated firms need: a data-access approver who is not the build owner. In a law firm that is usually the general counsel or risk partner. The harder problem is time. If utilisation is the firm's main performance measure, the owner's four protected hours a week will be the first casualty of a busy month. Set the protected time as a non-billable target with a code of its own, so its loss is visible. Part 3, *Gateway 0*, covers the rest.

**Tooling.** Buy seats for the people who pitch and the business development team that supports them. Set up automatic capture of email and meetings into the CRM for those people only, so the store fills without partners typing. A CRM that depends on partner data entry will not survive the first quarter.

**Context.** This is where the sector's qualification bites, and the next section covers it in detail. Connect the proposal library, the credentials database, the CRM and pitch correspondence. Do not connect matter files or engagement workpapers.

**Record.** The first decision class is pursue-or-pass, recorded with the reason, the owner, the expected fee and a date to check. The second is the fee estimate, with any discount beyond standard and its reason. Part 9, *The ten commercial decisions worth recording*, lists the fields. Record losses as carefully as wins: a firm that records only wins will learn that every pitch was a good idea.

**Reasoning.** The first agent should be the pitch preparation clerk: it reads the request for proposal, the client's history in the CRM, approved credentials and similar past pitch decisions, then drafts a preparation pack for the partner. It does not draft the proposal itself in the first month.

## The wall: confidences and conflicts

Every sector has context that must never be connected. In professional services it is the confidential information of one client, used for the benefit of another.

The rule is old. The SRA's guidance on conflicts explains that where a firm holds confidential information for one client that is material to another, it may act only if effective safeguards are in place. Those safeguards include separate fee earners and an established, structural separation within the firm, so that the information cannot pass between the lawyers acting for each client. Where the information cannot be protected, the firm must not act. Accounting and consulting firms work under comparable ethics codes and client contracts.

An assistant connected to a partner's whole inbox breaks that structure invisibly. A query for "our experience in logistics restructuring" may surface a live engagement for a competitor of the prospect, including figures the prospect would pay to see. The permissions on the files may technically allow it, because the partner can read both. The ethics rules do not.

Four rules keep the wall in the wiring rather than in a policy document:

- **Mirror the conflicts system.** Information barriers recorded in the conflicts or intake system become access rules in the context layer. If two teams are walled, their documents never appear in each other's retrieval.
- **Connect credentials, not matters.** Pitch agents read from an approved credentials library, written to be shareable, rather than from matter files.
- **Keep the record clean.** A pursue-or-pass record holds the reason in commercial terms ("sector fit, fee below our floor"), never client facts from another engagement.
- **Follow the vendor terms.** The Law Society's guidance on generative AI, updated in September 2025, advises firms not to put confidential data into free online tools, to check whether a tool trains on firm inputs, and to document inputs and outputs where a tool keeps no history.

> A partner can read both files. That does not mean an agent working for the partner should read them together.

## Where firms get stuck, and what to do about it

In our experience, professional services builds stall in three places, and each has a sector-specific fix.

**Gateway 0: the owner's time.** Covered above. The fix is a non-billable code and a named deputy, so the build survives a busy quarter.

**Gateway 1: approval as signature.** Partners already sign everything that goes to a client, so "nothing sends without a person" feels like an existing rule. The risk is the opposite of the one most sectors face. The approval exists, but it is a signature on a draft the partner did not read closely. *Ayinde* is the cautionary case: the citations were submitted under a professional's name. For AI-assisted pitch material, the approver confirms three things before anything leaves: every credential is approved for external use, every fee figure matches the estimate in the record, and no client is named without permission. Our piece *Approval rate measures fatigue too* explains why a near-100% approval rate should prompt a check rather than reassurance.

**Gateway 2: the dollar figure.** Professional services firms have an unusually good one: realisation. Record the expected fee when the pursue-or-pass decision is made. When the final bill goes out, write back the fee billed and collected. The gap between the two, by pitch type and discount level, is the first number the brain produces that a managing partner will act on. It often shows that some discounts that won work also lost money on it.

**Gateway 3: extending to delivery.** Only when the commercial record is trusted should the build extend to staffing and delivery. Even then, the walls stay. A staffing agent that sees engagement data must respect the same barriers as the pitch agent, and in a firm with active conflicts that may mean separate context layers for separate teams.

Illustrative example: an accounting and advisory firm records its pitch decisions

Decision
:   Record every pursue-or-pass decision on tenders above a set fee threshold, with the reason, the owner, the expected fee and a check date at final bill.

Reason and owner
:   Partners believed fixed-fee tenders in one sector were profitable; nobody had compared quoted fees with realised fees. Owned by the head of business development, with the risk partner as data-access approver.

What changed
:   The first pitch preparation agent reads only the approved credentials library and the record, never engagement files. After two quarters, realisation data showed one tender category consistently realising well below estimate, and the firm raised its floor fee for that category.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size accounting and advisory firm of around 140 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The order holds, with walls built in early.** Confidentiality and conflict barriers belong in the context layer from day one.
- **Start at the pitch.** Pursue-or-pass decisions and fee estimates are frequent, gradable and defended by a practice head.
- **Protect the owner's time explicitly.** In a utilisation-driven firm, unprotected build time disappears first.
- **Use realisation as the dollar figure.** Expected fee at pitch, realised fee at final bill, joined in one record.
- **Treat partner sign-off as a control, not a ritual.** Approval means checking credentials, figures and names.

Gateway card

### Before a professional services firm connects its first agent

- A named owner with a non-billable code for protected hours, and a deputy
- A data-access approver who is not the build owner
- Information barriers from the conflicts system mirrored in the context layer
- An approved credentials library the agent reads instead of matter files
- Pursue-or-pass decisions recorded with expected fee and a check date
- A three-point approval check for anything sent to a client or prospect
